description: issue #953: a `wait` whose pause is longer than the run can afford raises ol-limit/instruction-budget instead of occupying the execution thread for arbitrary wall-time. Before #953 the whole pause was ONE charged statement no matter how many ticks it ran, so `wait` was the only form in the language that was cancellable but NOT budgeted -- half of the pair spec/execution-model.md#execution-safety says safety comes from ("`forever` is therefore safe only because it is cancellable and budgeted"), and the one form that could pass every limit while running unbounded work for a single learner-written token. Measured on the saga tip before the fix, at the default budget: a bare `wait N` completed cleanly with two events and no diagnostic for every N up to 200,000,000 (the search was stopped there; no gate existed at all, so the true ceiling was unbounded), and `wait 999999999` blocked the execution thread for 413 seconds. Each tick is now one charged instruction -- the same unit a `forever` pass is, and one this runtime does comparable work for: a tick advances the clock, polls cancellation, enqueues host input and claims all four handler buckets. The trailing `primitive` event is absent BECAUSE the pause did not complete (spec/interaction-events.md: "wait emits a `primitive` event after the pause completes"), and the partial trace up to the cutoff is preserved rather than discarded, exactly as core-language/execution/forever-instruction-budget-limit does for `forever`. The `ol-limit` carries the paused instruction's own span. A small `instructionBudget` keeps the trace readable while pinning the same property the default budget of 1,000,000 does; the in-budget twin wait-in-budget-no-limit runs the same shape under the SAME budget and completes cleanly, so this diagnostic is not merely a budget too small for any program.
